title: Check a parallel-jaw friction grasp and read its contact trace
scope: Analytic quasi-static Coulomb-friction hold condition for a two-pad parallel-jaw grasp (minimum squeeze, safety factor, friction cone) and a threshold retention observer over a declared synthetic force trace; no physics engine, soft contact, torsional friction, multi-finger grasp or hardware

routeNotes.lift-feasibility: 2μN ≥ m(g + a) with g = 9.81: per-pad friction share, minimum squeeze, safety factor, largest holding acceleration and mass, with unit conversion.
routeNotes.retention-trace: Friction-cone test on pad readings, then contact/slip/release events from a synthetic (cmd, fn, ft) trace with the closed cone edge inside, and inferring mass or friction change from the hold and slip samples.

items.prompt: Two flat parallel pads squeeze a rigid box from opposite sides. Each pad presses with normal force N and has Coulomb friction coefficient μ, so one pad can carry a tangential (friction) force of at most μN; the two pads share the load equally. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and treat the model as quasi-static: the box is lifted straight up with upward acceleration a (positive up), so the two pads together must supply a total friction force of m(g + a). A bench gripper lifts a 0.8 kg box at constant speed (a = 0), with μ = 0.6 on both pads. Find the friction force each pad must carry and the smallest normal force N per pad at which the box just holds. Tolerance ±0.001 N for both.

fields.label: Friction force each pad must carry (N)
Smallest holding normal force N per pad (N)

items.solution: At constant speed the total friction must equal the weight: m(g + a) = 0.8 · 9.81 = 7.848 N. The two pads share it, so each carries 3.924 N. A pad carries at most μN, so just holding means μN = 3.924 and N = 3.924 / 0.6 = 6.54 N per pad. Check: 2 · 0.6 · 6.54 = 7.848 N.
hints: Start from the vertical force balance on the box: the friction from both pads must cancel the weight. Decide first how that total is shared between the two pads, then relate one pad's share to μN.
Compute the weight m·g in newtons, halve it for the per-pad friction (your first answer), and then set that per-pad friction equal to the largest a pad can carry, μN, and solve for N.

At constant speed the total friction must equal the weight: m(g + a) = 0.8 · 9.81 = 7.848 N. The two pads share it, so each carries 3.924 N. A pad carries at most μN, so just holding means μN = 3.924 and N = 3.924 / 0.6 = 6.54 N per pad. Check: 2 · 0.6 · 6.54 = 7.848 N.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: letting one pad carry the whole weight gives friction 7.848 N and N = 13.08 N; using g = 10 gives 4 N and N = 6.6667 N; multiplying by μ instead of dividing gives N = 2.3544 N. See the bridge parallel-jaw-friction (force balance), then try a fresh X35 item.

items.prompt: Two flat parallel pads squeeze a rigid box from opposite sides. Each pad presses with normal force N and has Coulomb friction coefficient μ, so one pad can carry a tangential (friction) force of at most μN; the two pads share the load equally. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and treat the model as quasi-static: the box is lifted straight up with upward acceleration a (positive up), so the two pads together must supply a total friction force of m(g + a). A pick-and-place cell squeezes a 1.5 kg box with N = 12 N per pad and μ = 0.4, and plans to lift it with a = 2 m/s². Define the safety factor S as the friction the two pads can supply, 2μN, divided by the friction needed, m(g + a); S ≥ 1 means the grasp holds. Compute S for the planned lift, and the largest upward acceleration a_max (m/s²) at which this same squeeze still holds; a negative a_max would mean the box cannot even be held still. Tolerance ±0.001 for both.
items.solution: Capacity: 2μN = 2 · 0.4 · 12 = 9.6 N. Demand at a = 2: m(g + a) = 1.5 · 11.81 = 17.715 N. S = 9.6 / 17.715 = 0.541914 < 1, so the planned lift slips. The limit solves 2μN = m(g + a_max): a_max = 2μN/m − g = 6.4 − 9.81 = -3.41 m/s². It is negative: this squeeze cannot hold the box even at rest.
hints: Both quantities compare the same two forces: the friction capacity 2μN and the friction demand m(g + a). S is their ratio at the planned a; a_max is the a that makes them equal.
Evaluate the capacity 2μN first. Divide it by m(g + a) with a = 2 for S. For a_max rearrange 2μN = m(g + a) to isolate a, and keep the sign when the result is below zero.

Capacity: 2μN = 2 · 0.4 · 12 = 9.6 N. Demand at a = 2: m(g + a) = 1.5 · 11.81 = 17.715 N. S = 9.6 / 17.715 = 0.541914 < 1, so the planned lift slips. The limit solves 2μN = m(g + a_max): a_max = 2μN/m − g = 6.4 − 9.81 = -3.41 m/s². It is negative: this squeeze cannot hold the box even at rest.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: counting only one pad gives S = 0.271 and a_max = −6.61; dropping a from S and g from a_max gives S = 0.6524 and a_max = 6.4; reporting g − 2μN/m gives a_max = 3.41. See the bridge parallel-jaw-friction (hold condition), then try a fresh X35 item.

items.prompt: Two flat parallel pads squeeze a rigid box from opposite sides. Each pad presses with normal force N and has Coulomb friction coefficient μ, so one pad can carry a tangential (friction) force of at most μN; the two pads share the load equally. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and treat the model as quasi-static: the box is lifted straight up with upward acceleration a (positive up), so the two pads together must supply a total friction force of m(g + a). A gripper squeezes with N = 12 N per pad on pads with μ = 0.35 and lifts at a = 2.2 m/s². (a) What is the largest box mass (kg) this squeeze can lift without slipping? (b) A new part weighs 900 g (its mass is 900 grams, not kilograms) and the same lift is planned with the same μ: what is the smallest normal force N per pad (N) that holds it? Tolerance ±0.001 for each.

fields.label: Smallest holding N per pad for the 900 g part (N)

items.solution: The hold limit 2μN = m(g + a) gives m_max = 2μN/(g + a) = 2 · 0.35 · 12 / 12.01 = 8.4 / 12.01 = 0.699417 kg. For the 900 g part, convert to 0.9 kg and solve for N: N = m(g + a)/(2μ) = 0.9 · 12.01 / 0.7 = 10.809 / 0.7 = 15.441429 N per pad.
hints: Both parts use the same hold equation 2μN = m(g + a), with g + a = 12.01 m/s² here; part (a) solves it for the mass, part (b) for the squeeze force. Convert grams to kilograms before using it.
For (a) divide the capacity 2μN by g + a. For (b) turn 900 g into kilograms, multiply by g + a to get the friction needed, and divide by 2μ.

The hold limit 2μN = m(g + a) gives m_max = 2μN/(g + a) = 2 · 0.35 · 12 / 12.01 = 8.4 / 12.01 = 0.699417 kg. For the 900 g part, convert to 0.9 kg and solve for N: N = m(g + a)/(2μ) = 0.9 · 12.01 / 0.7 = 10.809 / 0.7 = 15.441429 N per pad.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: using g instead of g + a gives 0.8563 kg and N = 12.6129 N; counting one pad only gives 0.3497 kg and N = 30.8829 N; using 900 as if it were kilograms gives N = 15441.43 N. See the bridge parallel-jaw-friction (units and hold equation), then try a fresh X35 item.

items.prompt: A force sensor on one gripper pad of a simulated pick reads a normal force of 6.0 N (pressing on the box) and a tangential force of 4.2 N along the pad. The pad has Coulomb friction coefficient μ = 0.6. The friction cone is the set of pad forces with |ft| ≤ μ·fn. Compute the largest tangential force this pad can carry at fn = 6.0 N, the friction coefficient the reading demands (ft/fn), and by how much (N) the reading exceeds the pad's capacity (use a negative number if it is below). Tolerance ±0.001 for each.
items.solution: The capacity is μ·fn = 0.6 · 6.0 = 3.6 N. The reading demands ft/fn = 4.2 / 6.0 = 0.7, larger than μ = 0.6, so the force is outside the cone and the pad slips. The excess is 4.2 − 3.6 = 0.6 N.
hints: Friction on one pad is limited by the normal force pressing on it: the cone compares |ft| with μ times fn. Only this one pad is involved, not the pair.
Multiply μ by fn for the capacity, divide the tangential reading by the normal reading for the demanded coefficient, and subtract the capacity from the reading for the excess.
The capacity is μ·fn = 0.6 · 6.0 = 3.6 N. The reading demands ft/fn = 4.2 / 6.0 = 0.7, larger than μ = 0.6, so the force is outside the cone and the pad slips. The excess is 4.2 − 3.6 = 0.6 N.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: doubling the capacity for two pads gives 7.2 N and an excess of −3 N (wrongly inside the cone); multiplying μ by ft gives 2.52 N; inverting the ratio gives 1.4286. See the bridge parallel-jaw-friction (friction cone), then try a fresh X35 item.

items.prompt: A retention observer reads a synthetic gripper trace. Each sample is (cmd, fn, ft): cmd = 0 means the gripper is commanded closed and 1 commanded open; fn and ft are the measured normal and tangential force per pad in newtons. Samples are numbered from 0. The pads have μ = 0.5 and the contact threshold is 1.0 N. Rules: while closed and not yet in contact, the first sample with fn ≥ 1.0 N is the event "contact". While in contact, the first sample with |ft| > μ·fn (strictly greater) is the event "slip". The first sample with cmd = 1 while in contact is the event "release". (If no contact has happened after 3 consecutive closed samples the observer reports "empty"; a contact on the third sample counts as contact, not empty.) Trace, sample index: (cmd, fn, ft): 0: (0, 0, 0); 1: (0, 0.4, 0); 2: (0, 1, 0.4); 3: (0, 3, 1); 4: (0, 3, 1.5); 5: (0, 3, 1.8); 6: (0, 3, 1.2); 7: (1, 2, 0.5). Give the sample index of the first contact, the first slip and the release.
items.solution: Contact: sample 1 has fn = 0.4 N < 1.0 N, sample 2 has fn = 1.0 N ≥ 1.0 N, so contact is at index 2 (and it is the third closed sample, so not empty). Slip: μ·fn = 0.5 · 3.0 = 1.5 N from sample 3 on. Sample 3 has ft = 1.0 and sample 4 has ft = 1.5, equal to the capacity, which is not strictly greater, so no slip. Sample 5 has ft = 1.8 > 1.5: slip at index 5 (sample 6 returns inside the cone). Release: sample 7 is the first with cmd = 1 while in contact: index 7.
hints: Walk the samples in order and keep two things: whether you are in contact, and the cone limit μ·fn for the current fn. Each event is the first sample where its own rule becomes true.

Find the first sample with fn at least the threshold (apply the comparison exactly as the rule states it), then compare |ft| with μ·fn = 0.5·fn after that sample, and finally look for the first open command.

Contact: sample 1 has fn = 0.4 N < 1.0 N, sample 2 has fn = 1.0 N ≥ 1.0 N, so contact is at index 2 (and it is the third closed sample, so not empty). Slip: μ·fn = 0.5 · 3.0 = 1.5 N from sample 3 on. Sample 3 has ft = 1.0 and sample 4 has ft = 1.5, equal to the capacity, which is not strictly greater, so no slip. Sample 5 has ft = 1.8 > 1.5: slip at index 5 (sample 6 returns inside the cone). Release: sample 7 is the first with cmd = 1 while in contact: index 7.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: requiring fn strictly above 1.0 N gives (contact, slip, release) = (3, 5, 7); calling ft = μ·fn a slip gives (2, 4, 7); numbering samples from 1 gives (3, 6, 8). The cone edge is inside the closed cone; see the observer rules in the bridge parallel-jaw-friction, then try a fresh X35 item.

items.prompt: Two flat parallel pads squeeze a rigid box from opposite sides. Each pad presses with normal force N and has Coulomb friction coefficient μ, so one pad can carry a tangential (friction) force of at most μN; the two pads share the load equally. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and treat the model as quasi-static: the box is lifted straight up with upward acceleration a (positive up), so the two pads together must supply a total friction force of m(g + a). A simulated pick squeezes an unknown box with N = 9.0 N per pad on dry pads (μ = 0.5). The observer trace is (cmd, fn, ft) per sample, forces per pad in newtons, samples numbered from 0, contact threshold 1.0 N, slip when |ft| > μ·fn: 0: (0, 0, 0); 1: (0, 9, 0); 2: (0, 9, 3.924); 3: (0, 9, 3.924); 4: (0, 9, 5.124); 5: (0, 9, 5.124); 6: (1, 0, 0). Samples 2 and 3 are the hold phase with the box stationary (a = 0); the lift at a = 3 m/s² starts at sample 4. (a) Give the index of the "slip" event. (b) Treat the hold-phase tangential reading as the true load share of each pad and find the box mass (kg). (c) With that mass and the lift at a = 3 m/s², what is the smallest normal force N per pad (N) that holds on dry pads (μ = 0.5), and (d) if the pads become oily with μ = 0.4? Tolerance ±0.001 for each.

fields.label: Box mass from the hold phase (kg)
Smallest holding N per pad, μ = 0.5 (N)
Smallest holding N per pad, μ = 0.4 (N)

items.solution: (a) μ·fn = 0.5 · 9.0 = 4.5 N. Samples 2 and 3 read ft = 3.924 N ≤ 4.5 N, inside the cone, but sample 4 reads 5.124 N > 4.5 N: slip at index 4 (contact was at index 1). (b) Two pads carry the weight at a = 0, so m g = 2 · 3.924 = 7.848 N and m = 7.848 / 9.81 = 0.8 kg. (c) Demand at the lift: m(g + a) = 0.8 · 12.81 = 10.248 N; N = 10.248 / (2 · 0.5) = 10.248 N per pad, more than the 9.0 N used, consistent with the slip. (d) With μ = 0.4: N = 10.248 / (2 · 0.4) = 12.81 N per pad.
hints: The trace itself answers (a) by the cone test on each closed sample after contact; the hold-phase reading then turns into a mass through the weight, and that mass feeds the hold equation 2μN = m(g + a) for the two squeeze forces.

Compare each ft with 0.5·9.0 to find the slip sample. For the mass, double the per-pad hold reading (two pads) and divide by g. Then multiply the mass by g + 3 to get the lift demand and divide by 2μ for each coefficient.

(a) μ·fn = 0.5 · 9.0 = 4.5 N. Samples 2 and 3 read ft = 3.924 N ≤ 4.5 N, inside the cone, but sample 4 reads 5.124 N > 4.5 N: slip at index 4 (contact was at index 1). (b) Two pads carry the weight at a = 0, so m g = 2 · 3.924 = 7.848 N and m = 7.848 / 9.81 = 0.8 kg. (c) Demand at the lift: m(g + a) = 0.8 · 12.81 = 10.248 N; N = 10.248 / (2 · 0.5) = 10.248 N per pad, more than the 9.0 N used, consistent with the slip. (d) With μ = 0.4: N = 10.248 / (2 · 0.4) = 12.81 N per pad.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: letting one pad carry the weight gives m = 0.4 kg; using the lift acceleration in the hold phase gives m = 0.6126 kg; ignoring the friction change gives the same N = 10.248 N for both coefficients; forgetting the lift acceleration gives N = 7.848 N and 9.81 N. See the slip-to-mass reasoning in the bridge parallel-jaw-friction, then try a fresh X35 item.
